title: Judging Ageing Potential
quiz.0.question: Of the four chemical pillars for judging ageing potential, which is the most important "first line of defence"?
quiz.0.explanation: Acidity (low pH) is the first line of defence for ageing: it inhibits microbial growth, protects colour and keeps freshness — a feature shared by all long-lived wines.
quiz.1.question: Which statement best describes how storage temperature affects the speed of ageing?
quiz.1.options.0: Temperature has little effect; just avoid freezing
quiz.1.options.1: The warmer, the faster the ageing: reaction rates roughly double for every rise of about 10°C
quiz.1.options.3: Heat actually speeds up beneficial ageing
quiz.1.explanation: According to chemical kinetics, reaction rates roughly double for every rise of about 10°C. So ageing at 20°C is clearly faster than at 14°C, and heat also brings unbalanced, coarse ageing; a stable cool temperature markedly slows ageing and lets the wine develop in balance.
quiz.2.question: Tasting a 15-year-old Barolo, you find a brick-red colour + orange rim + prominent leather and tobacco. What does this mean?
quiz.2.options.0: It is past its peak and declining
quiz.2.options.1: It is at its peak of maturity, the best time to drink
quiz.2.options.2: It is not yet mature and needs more cellaring
quiz.2.explanation: Brick red + an orange rim + prominent leather and tobacco are typical signs of a mature Barolo, showing the wine has reached its peak of maturity — an excellent time to drink it.
quiz.3.question: Using a practical scoring checklist for ageing potential, which wine is most likely to score highest?
quiz.3.options.0: A white with low acid, low tannin, low alcohol and no oak ageing
quiz.3.options.1: A red with high acid, high tannin, high alcohol and oak ageing
quiz.3.options.2: A sweet white with low acid, high sugar and high alcohol
quiz.3.options.3: A light red with high acid, low tannin and low alcohol
quiz.3.explanation: High acidity (low pH), high tannin, high alcohol and oak ageing — with all four positive factors present, the wine has the strongest pillars for ageing, typical of wines with high ageing potential.
slides.0.title: Judging Ageing Potential
slides.0.subtitle: Scientifically assessing the ageing ability of Italian wines
slides.1.title: The Four Chemical Pillars: The Science of Ageing Potential
slides.1.content:
Ageing potential is not mysticism but a measurable chemical system. Master the four pillars and you can scientifically predict how any Italian wine will age.

💧 Acidity (first pillar): low pH (high acidity) is the first line of defence for ageing. It inhibits microbes, protects colour and keeps freshness. Target pH 3.2-3.5
🍇 Tannin (second pillar): polyphenol polymerisation is the heart of red-wine ageing. Good tannins soften and add complexity as they polymerise; coarse tannins do not improve
🔬 Alcohol (third pillar): 13.5-15% ABV is the ideal range for ageing. Too low gives little protection; too high (over 15.5%) may mask finesse
🪵 Oak ageing (fourth pillar): gentle oxidation integrates tannins and adds structure. But too much new oak can mask terroir

⚖️ What Italy's Longest-Lived Grapes Have in Common

Nebbiolo (Barolo/Barbaresco): low pH (about 3.2-3.5), very high tannin, 13.5-15% ABV — all three pillars present
Sangiovese Grosso (Brunello): a similar acid and tannin structure, but slightly fewer anthocyanins, relying on acidity for longer ageing
slides.2.title: Ageing-Potential Rankings of Italy's Main Grapes
slides.2.content:
🥇 Gold (25-50 years)

Nebbiolo / Sagrantino / Brunello Sangiovese

All three pillars present (acid + tannin + alcohol) | e.g. Barolo, Barbaresco, Brunello di Montalcino, Sagrantino di Montefalco

🥈 Silver (15-25 years)

Aglianico / Amarone Corvina / Chianti Classico Sangiovese

High tannin and acidity | e.g. Taurasi, Amarone, Chianti Classico Gran Selezione, Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Riserva

🥉 Bronze (8-15 years)

Montepulciano / Nero d'Avola / Cannonau

Medium ageing potential | e.g. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, Nero d'Avola Riserva, Cannonau di Sardegna Riserva

🏅 Standard (3-8 years)

Barbera / Dolcetto / most white grapes

Best drunk early | e.g. Barbera d'Asti, Dolcetto d'Alba (exceptions: top whites such as Fiano, Verdicchio and Timorasso can age 10-15+ years)
slides.3.title: Sight, Smell and Palate: Quickly Judging a Wine's Stage
slides.3.content:
A Three-Sense Quick Diagnosis

👁️ Visual clues
Young (0-5 years): deep purple-red, bright rim
Mature (10-20 years): brick red, increasingly orange rim
Old (20+ years): pale brick to amber + brown rim + sediment is normal
⚠️ Browning too early = an oxidation problem
👃 Aroma clues
Young: fresh berries, violet, oaky vanilla
Mature: leather, tobacco, mushroom, black truffle
Peak: complex spice + aged fruit + minerality
⚠️ Vinegar or (excessive) stable notes = a quality fault
👅 Palate clues
Young: tight tannins, fresh acidity, fruit-led
Mature: silky tannins, acidity still fresh and supportive
Peak: everything perfectly integrated, a very long finish
⚠️ Acidity gone + withered fruit = past its peak
slides.4.title: How Storage Conditions Affect the Speed of Ageing
slides.4.content:
The same wine stored in different conditions can differ greatly in how fast it ages and in quality. Below is an analysis of the key factors affecting the speed of ageing.

🌡️ Temperature (most critical): for every rise of about 10°C, chemical reaction rates roughly double, and heat also causes unbalanced ageing. Cool temperatures markedly slow ageing. Ideal range: 12-15°C
💧 Humidity: ideally 70-80%. Too low (below 50%) dries and shrinks the cork; too high (over 85%) causes mould and label damage
🌑 Light: light (especially daylight and UV) is a catalyst for photo-oxidation; long exposure speeds up ageing and creates "light-struck" aromas
📳 Vibration: constant vibration disturbs sediment formation and destabilises tannin polymerisation; vibration from nearby roads or appliances is a common problem

A Practical Case: Storage Conditions Compared

Perfect cellar (constant 14°C) vs an ordinary home (22-28°C in summer): the same Barolo vintage after 10 years — the cellared bottle still has firm tannins, while the home-stored one may already be past its peak
Conclusion: before investing in wines from top estates, make sure you have suitable storage — otherwise drinking-style wines (Classico, Barbera) are better value
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: The four chemical pillars of ageing: acidity (the first line of defence), tannin, alcohol (13.5-15% ideal), oak ageing
slides.5.points.1: Nebbiolo has the greatest ageing potential in Italy: high acid + high tannin + high alcohol, potential 25-50 years
slides.5.points.2: Gold-tier grapes (25-50 years): Nebbiolo, Sagrantino, Brunello Sangiovese
slides.5.points.3: Silver-tier grapes (15-25 years): Aglianico (Taurasi), Amarone, Chianti Classico Gran Selezione
slides.5.points.4: Visual diagnosis: brick red + orange rim = maturing; premature browning = an oxidation problem
slides.5.points.5: Aroma diagnosis: leather + tobacco + truffle = maturity; excessive volatile acidity = a quality fault
slides.5.points.6: Temperature matters most: for every rise of about 10°C, ageing reactions roughly double; a stable cool temperature (12-15°C) lets the wine develop in balance
slides.5.points.7: Temperature stability matters more than the exact figure — fluctuation is the biggest killer of ageing
slides.5.points.8: Barolo's classic modern vintages: 2010 is hailed by many critics as the peak of the traditional style, often ranked alongside 2016
